title: Can Christians Have a High Sex Drive and Still Be Holy?
paragraphs: Can Christians Have a High Sex Drive and Still Be Holy?
What if the desire you keep asking God to remove is not the sin—and the real battle is over who gets to rule it?
There is a prayer some Christians are almost too embarrassed to pray.
“God… why am I like this?”
They love Jesus.
They read Scripture. They worship. They want a clean heart. They genuinely want to honor Christ with their bodies.
And yet sexual desire can feel incredibly strong.
Sometimes painfully strong.
So they begin wondering whether something must be spiritually wrong with them.
Maybe I’m not holy enough.
Maybe a mature Christian wouldn’t feel this much.
Maybe if I really loved Jesus, these desires would disappear.
Maybe God is disappointed that my body still wants what it wants.
And because churches sometimes speak extensively about sexual sin while saying comparatively little about sexual desire, believers can quietly begin treating the two as though they were identical.
They are not.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Scripture does not teach that holiness means becoming a person incapable of sexual desire.
Scripture teaches something far more demanding—and far more beautiful.
Your desires must come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That means the answer to the question, “Can Christians have a high sex drive and still be holy?” is yes.
But that “yes” needs the rest of the Bible wrapped around it.

A strong sexual appetite is not automatically sexual immorality. Neither is it automatically evidence of spiritual health. Desire is powerful, and like every powerful part of human life, it must be governed by God rather than enthroned as god.
Paul was not naïve about this.
Writing to believers in Corinth, he said:
“εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμεῖν ἢ πυροῦσθαι.”
“If they do not exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.”

The final Greek word is πυροῦσθαι (pyrousthai), from a verb meaning to burn or be set on fire. In context, Paul recognizes the reality of intense sexual passion rather than pretending mature believers never experience it.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “If you experience strong sexual desire, you obviously do not love God.”
He does not tell believers that possessing sexual passion itself makes them filthy.
He takes desire seriously enough to insist that it be handled within God's design.
And that changes the conversation.
Because perhaps you have spent years fighting the wrong enemy.
Perhaps you thought your sexuality itself was the monster when Scripture was calling you to confront something different: sexuality severed from obedience to God.

The Bible can speak positively about marital desire with a frankness that sometimes surprises modern Christians. Song of Songs describes physical attraction and marital longing without treating embodied desire itself as shameful. The woman can say of her beloved, “I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
That sentence belongs in the same Bible that commands sexual holiness.
Think about that.
God does not need to choose between holiness and marital passion.
We do.
We are the ones who sometimes imagine that “holy” must mean emotionally sterile, physically indifferent, embarrassed by sexuality and frightened of desire.
Scripture presents a richer picture.
Hebrews 13:4 reads in Greek:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed ἀμίαντος (amiantos)—undefiled, unpolluted, unstained. The verse then warns that God will judge sexual immorality and adultery.
Do not miss the contrast.
The marriage bed is not presented as inherently dirty.
It is presented as capable of being undefiled.
Christian holiness does not require married couples to apologize for enjoying the covenant intimacy God permits them to share.
But neither does the goodness of sexuality give us permission to redraw God's boundaries around it.
That is where our culture often makes the opposite mistake.
Some religious environments have acted as though desire itself were shameful.
Our surrounding culture frequently responds by acting as though desire itself were sovereign.
Jesus gives us neither option.
You are not commanded to worship your desires.
You are commanded to worship Christ.
And when Christ becomes Lord, even something as intimate as sexuality comes under His authority.
Paul says:
“τοῦτο γάρ ἐστιν θέλημα τοῦ Θεοῦ, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν…”
“This is the will of God, your sanctification…”
And what immediately follows?

That believers abstain from πορνεία (porneia), sexual immorality, and learn to live in holiness and honor rather than uncontrolled passion. The key word ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos) means sanctification or consecration—the life increasingly set apart to God.
Here is where this becomes painfully personal.
Holiness is not measured by how little temptation you experience.
Holiness is revealed in what you do when temptation arrives.
You can experience desire without giving desire permission to become your master.
You can notice beauty without mentally undressing someone.
You can experience attraction without feeding fantasy.
You can feel arousal without turning pornography into medication for loneliness.
You can be single and deeply sexual without believing another person's body is owed to you.
You can be married and passionately attracted to your spouse while remembering that marriage never transforms selfishness, coercion, exploitation, infidelity, or degradation into holiness.
The question is not merely, “How strong is my sex drive?”
The deeper question is:
Who owns it?
That question reaches places nobody else sees.
The browser history.
The private messages.
The lingering look.
The fantasy deliberately replayed.
The emotional affair nobody has named yet.
The pornography you promised would be “the last time.”
The person you keep contacting even though you know exactly where the conversation is heading.
The rationalization.
The secret.
The loneliness underneath the secret.
And Jesus goes there.
Not because He delights in humiliating you.
Because He intends to free the whole person.
In Matthew 5:28, Jesus says:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
The phrase concerns looking at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι—with the purpose or intent of lusting after her—and Jesus carries the issue all the way into the heart.
That matters because temptation and deliberate lust should not simply be collapsed into the same thing.
Seeing an attractive person is not identical to choosing to cultivate sexual possession of that person in your imagination.
An involuntary bodily response is not identical to deliberately feeding fantasy.
Being tempted is not the same thing as consenting to temptation.
Yet we should be equally careful not to use that distinction as a loophole.
Jesus refuses to let us define purity merely as “I didn't physically do anything.”
He walks straight through the locked door of outward respectability and asks what we are choosing in the heart.
That can hurt.
Because someone reading this has been technically “pure” in public while living another sexual life in private.
Nobody knows.
Your spouse may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your parents may not know.
Your friends see the Bible verses you post but not what happens after midnight.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is that you still love Jesus.
That is why the contradiction hurts so badly.
You fall.
You repent.
You promise.
You fall again.
Then shame whispers, “A real Christian wouldn't struggle like this.”
So you hide.
And hiding makes you lonely.
Loneliness makes temptation louder.
Temptation leads back toward the secret.
The secret produces more shame.
And eventually you become frightened that God must be tired of hearing your apologies.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that sexually spotless people can approach Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners need a Savior.
Paul once reminded the Corinthian church of devastating categories of sin—including sexual sin—and then spoke three astonishing words:
“Such were some of you.”
Then comes the language of grace: washed, sanctified, justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Christianity does not say sexual sin is insignificant.
Christianity says the blood of Christ is greater.
Jesus does not save us by pretending our chains are jewelry.
He calls sin what it is.
He calls us to repentance.
And then He does what shame never could.
He cleanses.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
That is the difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation whispers, “Hide from God because you are filthy.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light because Christ is merciful.”
Repentance does not mean merely feeling disgusted with yourself.
It means turning.
Turning from pornography.
Turning from adultery.
Turning from fornication.
Turning from sexual exploitation.
Turning from fantasies we intentionally nourish.
Turning from the secret relationship.
Turning from treating human beings made in God's image as bodies for consumption.
Turning from using sexuality as anesthesia for rejection, stress, insecurity, loneliness or pain.
And turning toward Jesus.
Because behavior modification without Christ merely produces another prison.
The goal is not to become someone who can boast, “Look how sexually disciplined I am.”
The goal is to become someone who can say:
“Jesus is Lord—even here.”
Especially here.
This is where self-control becomes beautiful.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:9 uses ἐγκρατεύονται (enkrateuontai), referring to exercising self-control. Paul recognizes burning passion, but he does not therefore enthrone passion.
Self-control is not the denial that desire exists.
It is the refusal to let desire become dictator.
A river without banks becomes destructive.
Banks do not prove the water is evil.
They give powerful water a course.
In a similar way, biblical boundaries do not exist because God despises human sexuality. They reveal that sexuality is significant enough to protect.
Your body matters.
The other person's body matters.
Marriage matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Your imagination matters.
Your future spouse matters.
Your present spouse matters.
And above everything else, Christ's lordship matters.
So yes, Christian husband, you may deeply desire your wife and still be holy.
Christian wife, you may deeply desire your husband and still be holy.
Single Christian, you may experience an intense sex drive and still sincerely belong to Jesus.
Someone who has experienced sexual failure can repent, receive Christ's forgiveness, walk in the light and pursue holiness.
Someone with a complicated sexual past is not beyond redemption.
Someone battling temptation is not required to pretend temptation does not exist.
But none of us gets to rename disobedience “authenticity” simply because the desire behind it feels powerful.
That is the tension mature Christianity refuses to abandon.
No shame for the existence of desire. No surrender to the dictatorship of desire.
And perhaps that sentence is why you found this article.
Maybe you have spent years begging God:
“Take this away.”
And perhaps part of His answer is not simply removal but sanctification.
“Give it to Me.”
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your hormones.
Your wounds.
Your memories.
Your phone.
Your private life.
Your sexuality.
Everything.
Not because Jesus wants less of you.
Because He died and rose again to redeem all of you.

If your struggle has become compulsive or feels impossible to interrupt, bringing it into wise, trustworthy Christian accountability can be an act of courage rather than defeat. Where appropriate, qualified professional counseling can also help address compulsive behavior, trauma, relational wounds, or patterns that simplistic advice does not resolve.
But do not wait until you feel worthy before approaching Christ.
You will wait forever.
Come because He is worthy.
Come confessing rather than performing.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
Come believing the Cross actually accomplished something.
The Christian message is not, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
It is that Christ saves sinners—and the grace that forgives us also begins teaching us a different way to live.
So when temptation comes tonight, your prayer may need to change.
Not merely:
“Jesus, make me stop feeling.”
But:

“Jesus, teach me to desire You more than I desire disobedience. Teach me to honor what You created without worshiping it. Teach me to see people as souls bearing Your image, not objects for my consumption. Teach me faithfulness. Teach me self-control. And when I fall, teach me to run toward Your mercy instead of deeper into hiding.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because God may start opening locked rooms.
He may expose habits.
He may confront relationships.
He may tell you to delete something you keep defending.
He may tell you to confess something.
He may require boundaries that initially feel severe.
He may teach a married couple to replace shame and selfishness with tenderness, faithfulness, communication and mutual honor.
He may teach a single believer that chastity is not proof that sexuality is evil, but testimony that Christ is worthy of obedience even when obedience costs something.
And somewhere in that process, you may discover something remarkable.
Holiness was never God amputating your humanity.
Holiness was God reclaiming it.
So stop measuring your spiritual condition merely by the intensity of your appetite.
Ask instead what happens to that appetite when Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Does desire kneel?
That is the battlefield.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they were never fighting alone.
Not as proof that you agree with every sentence.
Temptation has a strange ability to make us forget in darkness what we knew clearly in daylight.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a requirement for glorifying God—Scripture shows many ways believers glorify Him—but voluntarily supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work can itself become one meaningful expression of generosity and mission.
But whatever you do, never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness is not merchandise.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
At the Cross, Jesus did not merely offer better behavior to scandalous people.
He offered Himself.
And when sinners repent and trust Him, shame does not get the final word.
Pornography does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Your appetite does not get the final word.
Your worst night does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the sentence you need to carry away from this article is this:
Your desire may burn fiercely—but it was never meant to sit on the throne where only Christ belongs.
